name: Greenlandic (Kalaallisut)
variety: West Greenlandic (Kalaallisut), central dialect, in the 1973 orthography
sources: Fortescue, Michael (1984). West Greenlandic. London: Croom Helm.
Rischel, Jørgen (1974). Topics in West Greenlandic Phonology: Regularities Underlying the Phonetic Appearance of Wordforms in a Polysynthetic Language. Copenhagen: Akademisk Forlag.
Jacobsen, Birgitte (2000). The question of 'stress' in West Greenlandic: an acoustic investigation of rhythmicization, intonation, and syllable weight. Phonetica 57: 40-67.
Arnhold, Anja (2014). Prosodic structure and focus realization in West Greenlandic. In Jun, Sun-Ah (ed.), Prosodic Typology II. Oxford University Press, 216-251.
Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko (1992). Mora and Prosodic Coordination: A Phonetic Study of Japanese, Eskimo and Yoruba. Travaux de l'institut de linguistique de Lund 27. Lund University Press.
Nagano-Madsen, Yasuko (1993). Phrase-final intonation in West Greenlandic Eskimo. Working Papers 40: 145-155. Lund University, Department of Linguistics.
Mase, Hideo (1973). A study of the role of syllable and mora for the tonal manifestation in West Greenlandic. Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics, University of Copenhagen 7: 1-98.
Mase, Hideo; Rischel, Jørgen (1971). A study of consonant quantity in West Greenlandic. Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics, University of Copenhagen 5: 175-247.

Arnhold, Anja; Compton, Richard; Elfner, Emily (2018). Prosody and wordhood in South Baffin Inuktitut. Proceedings of WSCLA 21, University of British Columbia Working Papers in Linguistics. (summary of the West Greenlandic findings)
contrasts: three vowels /i u a/, each short or long
consonant length: nearly every consonant occurs single and geminate
no lexical stress and no lexical tone
allophony: before a uvular (/q ʁ/) vowels are lowered and retracted: /i/ to [e], [ɛ] or [ɐ] (written e), /u/ to [o] or [ɔ] (written o), /a/ to [ɑ]

a cluster written r plus consonant is pronounced as a long consonant with the vowel before it uvularised (arfeq, Qaqortoq with long [f], [t]); before a nasal some descriptions have a uvular nasal [ɴ], which is not found in all dialects
geminates of the voiced continuants are voiceless fricatives: /ll/ is [ɬː], /ɣɣ/ (written gg) is [çː] or [xː], /ʁʁ/ (written rr) is [χː], /vv/ (written ff) is [fː]
/t/ is affricated [t͡s] before /i/; the long affricate is written ts
/u/ is fronted to [ʉ] between coronal consonants
the stops are voiceless and unaspirated
the only diphthong, /ai/, occurs at the end of words; elsewhere older sequences of /a/ plus another vowel have become long [aː], while sequences such as ia, ua, iu, ui remain and count as two morae
phonotactics: no consonant clusters at the beginning or end of a word; inside a word only geminates and r plus consonant
words end in a vowel or in /p t k q/
long vowels count as two morae; a syllable closed by a consonant or the first half of a geminate is heavy
words are often very long because of polysynthesis; the letters e and o are written only before q and r

stress.rule: There is no lexical stress: acoustic studies find no regular stress cues, and impressions of prominence come from syllable weight and from the tone pattern at the end of the word or phrase.
stress.cues: duration follows the mora count, and pitch follows the phrase-final tone pattern; there is no intensity-based accent and no vowel reduction

rhythm.notes: The mora is both the unit of timing and the tone-bearing unit (Mase & Rischel 1971; Nagano-Madsen 1992; Jacobsen 2000).

length.notes: Long vowels and geminates each add a mora, and segment durations follow the mora count. No ratios are given here because the published figures could not be checked.

intonation.declarative: three tonal targets on the last three vowel morae of the word or phrase: high on the third from the end, low on the second, high on the last (HLH); in connected speech words show this pattern or reduced forms of it (HL, LH or flat); statements end high
intonation.yes_no_question: ends with low pitch: the final high is missing or the pitch falls on the last syllable
intonation.continuation: the final high of the HLH pattern
intonation.accent_shape: no pitch accents; tones are counted in morae from the end of the word or phrase
intonation.notes: Word contours vary with speaker, speech rate, style, word length and focus (Arnhold 2014).

tone.notes: Tones belong to the phrase, not to words; the tone-bearing unit is given for that phrase-level pattern.

phonation: geminate continuants are voiceless fricatives [ɬː çː χː fː]

problems: ll is a short [ɬ]: the length of the geminate is lost (illu, Kalaallit)
r before a consonant is spoken as a uvular trill or fricative followed by a short consonant (arfeq as [aʀfɛq], Qaqortoq as [qaqoʀtoq]); the literature has a long consonant after a uvularised vowel
/a/ is not retracted before q and r

prosody is stress-based: a primary stress is placed on the last long vowel or before a consonant cluster, otherwise on the final or the antepenultimate syllable; the HLH pattern on the last three morae is not modelled
questions get a rising tune, whereas Greenlandic yes/no questions end low and statements end high
word-final t after i is made an affricate [t͡ɕ] (Kalaallit, ippit); the literature has affrication of /t/ before /i/ only
final -ak, -ap, -at change the vowel to [æ], and final -ak ends in a voiced stop
all numbers are read in Danish, also 1 to 12, for which Greenlandic has its own words in the word list
good: gg and rr are long voiceless fricatives, ng is [ŋ] and nng is [ŋː]
long vowels and most geminates are lengthened
/q/ is a uvular stop, and e and o are given mid qualities where the spelling has them
equal length and loudness for stressed and unstressed syllables, which suits a language without stress

notes: Vowel formants, VOT and rhythm measures are left out because no figures were found that could be checked.
